First severe episode of melancholy, at about twenty.
Very severe return of his melancholy; averse to society.
Birthday prayer: fifty-five years of resolving.

claims.statement: Samuel Johnson was born at Lichfield, in Staffordshire, on September 18, 1709 (New Style), and was baptized the same day at St. Mary's church.
His father, Michael Johnson, a Lichfield bookseller and magistrate, had "a vile melancholy," which Johnson said he inherited and which "made him mad all his life, at least not sober."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Family history of melancholy as Johnson himself described it; recorded in his words, not as a modern diagnosis.

claims.statement: As a young child he had scrofula (the king's evil), which scarred his face and damaged his sight so that he did not see at all with one of his eyes; Boswell thought him only near-sighted. On the advice of the Lichfield physician Sir John Floyer, his mother took him to London to be touched by Queen Anne, without effect.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Scrofula was usually tuberculous lymphadenitis of the neck. Boswell does not say which eye was affected, or anything about his hearing.

claims.statement: In the college vacation of 1729, when he was about twenty, he was "overwhelmed with an horrible hypochondria," with irritation, fretfulness, impatience, dejection, gloom, and despair; he walked to Birmingham and back to fight it, wrote an account of his case in Latin for his godfather, the physician Dr. Swinfen, and was never afterwards perfectly relieved of it.
claims.clinical_interpretation: The first documented depressive episode; the basis for coding the modern depression as recurrent.

claims.statement: Insanity was "the object of his most dismal apprehension," and he at times feared he was losing his reason, when his friends saw no sign of it.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Supports psychoeducation in the modern episode; no psychosis is recorded.

claims.statement: His wife, Elizabeth, died on March 17, 1752 (Old Style), a loss that affected him with the deepest distress; he kept the anniversary of her death with prayer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Bereavement history; the cause of her death is not given in the cited source.

claims.statement: In 1764 he had "a very severe return of the hypochondriack disorder": though he loved company he became entirely averse to society, and his friend Dr. Adams found him "sighing, groaning, talking to himself, and restlessly walking from room to room," saying "I would consent to have a limb amputated to recover my spirits."
claims.clinical_interpretation: The anchor for the modern episode, a year later, at 55.

claims.statement: On his birthday in September 1764 he wrote a prayer: "I have now spent fifty-five years in resolving ... I have done nothing."
claims.clinical_interpretation: His own words of self-reproach; recorded as written, not scored.

claims.statement: Boswell described how, talking or musing in his chair, he held his head to one side toward his right shoulder and shook it, rocked his body backwards and forwards, and rubbed his left knee with his palm; between words he made sounds like chewing the cud, a half whistle, clucking like a hen, and "too, too, too" under his breath, and after an argument he blew out his breath "like a Whale." He also often talked to himself, muttering fragments of the Lord's Prayer.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary description of motor and vocal tics.

claims.statement: He had an "anxious care" to go in or out of a door by a certain number of steps, or with a particular foot first; Boswell saw him stop, count his steps, and go back to begin again when he had gone wrong, and Joshua Reynolds saw him go a long way round rather than cross a particular alley in Leicester Fields.

Alexander Pope, in a note, described him as having "an infirmity of the convulsive kind, that attacks him sometimes, so as to make him a sad Spectacle"; Boswell likened the movements to St. Vitus's dance; Reynolds wrote that they were improperly called convulsions, since he could sit motionless when told to, and thought them a habit of accompanying his thoughts with untoward actions, and that Johnson preferred any company to being alone, the great business of his life being "to escape from himself."
claims.clinical_interpretation: Contemporary opinions about the movements, including the distinction from chorea that a modern neurologist also makes.

claims.statement: When he was young his appearance was forbidding: he was lean, the scars of the scrofula were deeply visible, and his "convulsive starts and odd gesticulations" tended "to excite at once surprize and ridicule."
claims.clinical_interpretation: The documented stigma he faced; used only as recorded.

source_links.locator: account of his first meeting with Mrs. Porter

claims.statement: In 1979 the neurologist T. J. Murray concluded that Johnson's involuntary jerking movements and complex motor acts, involuntary vocalizations, and compulsive actions such as touching posts and measuring his steps constitute the symptom complex of Gilles de la Tourette syndrome, from which he suffered most of his life; later neurologists agreed, and historians have examined how the diagnosis was constructed.
claims.clinical_interpretation: Retrospective diagnosis widely accepted in the medical literature but necessarily unproven; the modern episode makes a synthetic diagnosis and does not assert that the historical man had it.

claims.statement: Johnson died in London on December 13, 1784, aged 75.
claims.clinical_interpretation: After the episode. The cause of death is not used.

synthetic_episode.teaching_objective: Primary care for a 55-year-old writer with a severe recurrent major depressive episode and lifelong, never-diagnosed motor and vocal tics: measurement-based depression care with the PHQ-9, an SSRI with dose adjustment and psychotherapy, a structured safety assessment with the 988 Suicide & Crisis Lifeline at every visit, recognizing adult Tourette syndrome and telling tics apart from chorea, assessing tic-related obsessive-compulsive symptoms, offering the Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics as initial treatment under the AAN guideline, and avoiding serotonergic and bleeding interactions when treating acute back pain in a patient on sertraline; built on the CMID depression monograph, the VA/DoD depression and suicide-risk guidelines, and the AAN 2019 tic guideline.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Johnson returns two weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg and is seen the same day by Dr. Hassan of neurology. He has taken it every morning. He had mild nausea for the first four days, which has passed, and no agitation or sleep change. His mood is no better yet; he still cannot write and has seen only one friend. The nurse called him after the first week, and he has had two psychotherapy sessions. He told Dr. Hassan about the movements and sounds he has made since boyhood, the urge he feels before each one, his habit of counting his steps at doorways and going back to start again if he gets it wrong, and his fear that all of this, with his low spirits, means he is going mad.

assessment_plan.assessment: The presenting tic disorder now has a diagnosis. Dr. Hassan confirms Tourette syndrome: multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic since childhood, present for decades, with premonitory urges and brief suppressibility, which distinguish tics from chorea. Yale Global Tic Severity Scale: motor 17, phonic 13, total tic score 30 of 50, impairment 20 of 50. Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale 13, mild, with counting and threshold rituals of the tic-related, just-right kind. No ADHD on screening. He was relieved to hear that tics are not madness

hpi.narrative: Mr. Johnson returns six weeks after starting sertraline 50 mg. He is a little better: he has written letters, though not his book, and walked out with a friend twice. He still wakes in the early morning with dread and reproaches himself for idleness. He has had five psychotherapy sessions and the first two sessions of behavioral therapy for tics, in which he is learning to notice the urge before the head-shaking tic and to answer it with a competing movement. He has no side effects.

hpi.narrative: Mr. Johnson returns five weeks after sertraline was increased to 100 mg. He is writing most mornings again and dines with friends several times a week. He wakes less often in dread. He has mild night sweats and no other side effects. He has had six of eight sessions of behavioral therapy for tics and uses the competing response for the head-shaking tic in company; the clucking sounds are less frequent. There was no check two weeks after the dose increase.

referral.question: Lifelong motor and vocal tics with ritual counting and stepping behaviors, never formally diagnosed, in a 55-year-old writer now in a severe recurrent depressive episode. Please confirm the diagnosis, exclude other movement disorders, assess obsessive-compulsive symptoms, and advise whether and how the tics should be treated alongside his depression
referral.urgency: Routine, within two weeks, on the same day as his two-week depression check
referral.pertinent_history: Since childhood: head turning toward the right shoulder with shaking, trunk rocking, rubbing of the left knee, sudden limb movements, clucking and half-whistling sounds, muttered phrases, and forceful exhalations, which strangers have long stared at and ridiculed. Rituals of counting his steps at doorways and going back to repeat them. Never assessed or treated. Now in a severe recurrent depressive episode (PHQ-9 21, item 9 scored 0; GAD-7 12; MDQ 3, negative), with a first episode at about twenty; structured safety assessment shows no suicidal thoughts; sertraline 50 mg daily and weekly psychotherapy started today. Fears he is losing his reason; no psychotic symptoms. Blindness of the left eye since childhood scrofula. No alcohol. Results today: sodium 140 mmol/L, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, vitamin B12 412 pg/mL, hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, ALT 24 U/L
questions: Do these movements and sounds meet criteria for Tourette syndrome, and is any other movement disorder, such as chorea, likely?
Are his rituals obsessive-compulsive disorder or tic-related, and do they need separate treatment?
Should his tics be treated now, and if so, with behavioral therapy or medication?
Does sertraline affect his tics, and which tic medicines should be avoided or used with it?
How should tic severity be measured and followed?

consultant_note.history: Mr. Johnson, a 55-year-old writer, is seen at the request of Dr. Bell. He describes movements and sounds since he was a boy: turning and shaking his head toward the right shoulder, rocking, rubbing his left knee, sudden jerks of a leg, clucking, half-whistles, a repeated "too, too" under his breath, muttering, and blowing out his breath after he has spoken. Each is preceded by an urge, like an itch, that the act relieves. He can hold them back for a short time, with growing discomfort. They wax and wane, are worse when he is idle, alone, anxious, or tired, and almost vanish when he is absorbed in talk or writing. He counts his steps at doorways and must begin again if he gets it wrong, until it feels right; he does not fear harm if he does not. He has never had these assessed. No head injury, infections with chorea in childhood, stimulant or antipsychotic use, or family history of a movement disorder is known. Two weeks on sertraline 50 mg with mild nausea that has passed. He fears the movements and his low spirits mean he is going mad
consultant_note.data_reviewed: Dr. Bell's intake note with PHQ-9 21, GAD-7 12, MDQ 3, and the safety assessment. Intake results: sodium 140 mmol/L, potassium 4.3 mmol/L, creatinine 0.98 mg/dL, eGFR 91, glucose 94 mg/dL, TSH 2.1 mIU/L, vitamin B12 412 pg/mL, hemoglobin 14.6 g/dL, ALT 24 U/L. Today's PHQ-9 19. Structured scales today: Yale Global Tic Severity Scale motor 17, phonic 13, total tic score 30 of 50, impairment 20 of 50 (global 50 of 100); Yale-Brown Obsessive Compulsive Scale 13; adult ADHD self-report screen negative

exam.finding: Alert, articulate, and slowed; mood low; no psychosis
No light perception in the left eye with a relative afferent pupillary defect; otherwise normal; eye movements full
Normal tone and strength; no rigidity, bradykinesia, tremor, or dystonia

Brief, stereotyped head turns with shaking, trunk rocking, knee rubbing, and limb jerks, with clucking, half-whistles, and forceful exhalations; suppressed for about a minute on request; no flowing, random chorea between them
Symmetric reflexes; normal finger-nose and heel-shin; normal gait and tandem walk

assessment.assessment: Multiple motor tics and at least one vocal tic, beginning in childhood and lasting decades, with premonitory urges, temporary suppressibility, and waxing and waning course. This meets criteria for Tourette syndrome. The movements are stereotyped and preceded by an urge, unlike chorea, which is random and flowing; the examination is otherwise normal, and no imaging or further tests are needed. The tics are moderate and cause real social impairment

Counting and threshold rituals driven by a need for things to feel just right, with a mild Y-BOCS of 13, are common in Tourette syndrome. They do not need separate treatment now; sertraline treats obsessive-compulsive symptoms as well as depression, and they can be reassessed as his mood improves

Depression and anxiety commonly accompany Tourette syndrome and often cause more impairment than the tics themselves. Treating the depression comes first. Sertraline does not worsen tics. Tics are not a sign of mental decline, and telling him so matters

recommendations: Comprehensive Behavioral Intervention for Tics (CBIT) as the initial tic treatment: eight sessions over about ten weeks with a trained therapist, starting in about two weeks

No tic medication now; if tics remain impairing after CBIT, an alpha-2 agonist such as guanfacine is a first medication option, and aripiprazole or another agent would need cardiac and metabolic monitoring
Continue sertraline and adjust it for the depression as Dr. Bell plans; avoid adding serotonergic drugs such as tramadol without review
Yale Global Tic Severity Scale at three and six months, then yearly; reassess obsessive-compulsive symptoms when the depression has lifted
Psychoeducation about the nature and natural history of tics, for him and, if he wishes, for those he lives with
consultant_note.communication: Discussed with Dr. Bell, who saw him the same day. The diagnosis and plan were explained to Mr. Johnson, who was relieved to have a name for the movements and agreed to behavioral therapy
